articles.title: Burnham's plan to collaborate with social media creators
articles.summary: The new prime minister plans to work with influencers and social media creators to get his message out.
articles.body:
Andy Burnham is a past master at using social media to create a political brand - and it seems he has no plans to let up now that he is prime minister.

One Downing Street source told the BBC they planned to take a "more social first" and "authentic to Andy" approach, with "less high production, polished" content than might have been seen from a prime minister in the past.

This means we can expect more clips of Burnham in casual mode, chatting into a handheld phone or answering questions on policy in an apparently spontaneous fashion on X, Instagram or TikTok.

There will also be a focus on collaborations with social media creators.

In an earlier age, political leaders liked to court TV stars and other celebrities to help get their message out.

Now the Holy Grail is online influencers, who are seen as more authentic, and trusted, by hard-to-reach voters who don't watch much TV or read newspapers.

Sir Keir Starmer's government had already begun experimenting with giving access to influencers, with ministers appearing on some of the more popular channels.

Downing Street also held receptions for influencers and during Tim Allan's tenure as director of communications content creators were invited to Downing Street press conferences.

Some critics saw this is a way of avoiding serious scrutiny of polices in favour of softball questions from non-specialists.

But Burnham's advisers see collaborations with influencers as a way of getting the government's message to audiences it might not normally reach.

A Downing Street source said "the vast majority" of the public will not see or interact with content that is coming from government or the prime minister's social media channels.

In the hours before and after becoming prime minister, Burnham co-authored two posts on TikTok and Instagram, including a running video with Sir Mo Farah.

Young TikTokers were also invited to Downing Street to thank them for their work on his Makerfield by-election campaign.

One of the social channels Sir Keir Starmer appeared on was run by Ukrainian online personality Max Klymenko, who won TikTok Creator of the year for his viral "The Career Ladder" series, where he quizzes people about their job history.

Klymenko was first approached by Burnham's team around two months ago to collaborate on content.

His team filmed the video quizzing the former Greater Manchester mayor on his first job, before he entered politics, a week ago, then planned to post it on his first day as prime minister to capitalise on the buzz.

The creator's core audience are aged 18 to 24, according to his team, while the majority of people who watch his content are aged between 25 and 30.

A member of his team pointed out this is far younger than the audience for a traditional TV interview, while his cumulative subscriber and follower count across TikTok, Instagram, YouTube and Facebook is more than 16.3 million accounts.

While there is some paid-for content on his pages, Klymenko said no payment or contract was exchanged with Burnham's team and they did not request changes to the content before it was posted.

Meanwhile, Sir Mo Farah's uploads, running while discussing sport, education and mental health with Burnham, went to his three million followers across YouTube, TikTok and Instagram, a far bigger reach than the prime minister's personal channels.

Andy Burnham Went Online, and Got Into No 10

Ros Atkins reports on how the new PM uses social media to get his message across.

The strategy is the brainchild of Abby Tomlinson, who ran Burnham's digital communications during the by-election, and who the BBC can confirm has been kept on for a new role in Burnham's administration.

She began her career in social media aged 17 by starting a "Milifandom" campaign on social media for Ed Miliband over a decade ago.

In more recent years, she has worked in digital communications for the Labour Party, and for Keir Starmer in Number10 before quitting last year.

Tomlinson has been credited with how Burnham connected with voters across platforms in recent months.

The new PM has rationed interviews with traditional media since returning to Parliament, in favour of vlogs, a question and answer session on Reddit and X posts clapping back at political opponents.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch took to Reddit to urge him to "come out from hiding, face a proper press conference and submit yourself to scrutiny and some tough questions".

Burnham responded to it by saying it had only been two weeks since he faced questions from "74,000 members of the public of Makerfield".

Another key strand of Burnham's campaigning strategy has been connecting with and organising grassroots social media activists.

Among the politicians and staffers invited to stand outside Number 10 to watch Burnham become prime minister on Monday were teenage TikTokers whose video edits have brought him to a new social media audience.

Between them, Will, Lottie, Megan, Ellen and Poppy, all aged between 17 and 19 have racked up millions of likes on TikTok, and across platforms share memes, trends and nostalgic edits of New Labour footage, including of Burnham's time in office.

The Labour activists were invited to canvass with him and make edits of his time on the Makerfield by-election campaign trail in a language and style that resonates with people online.

One way they got thousands of likes was by getting him to sign and pose with red pre-made cocktails popular with Gen Z.

Megan Cassidy, 19, from Havering, started making Labour content a year ago and said it was "surreal" to have found herself at Downing Street: "I really felt like I was witnessing history around me".

The young Labour activists said they were given access to Burnham and footage of him by his team, but are not paid and can choose to edit the material how they like.

They saw it as an opportunity to gain ground from social media savvy parties like Reform, whose leader Nigel Farage has an exponentially bigger following on social media, and the Greens who have experienced large growth in recent months.

It helped that Burnham was "natural" and happy to spontaneously appear in content, they told the BBC.

"I do think he gets it, absolutely compared to other politicians, compared to Starmer for example, I think he's a lot more charismatic," said Megan.

articles.title: Grant Shapps blocked from standing again for the Conservatives
articles.summary: Kemi Badenoch tells the BBC she leads a "new party full of new people" as ex-MP is rejected as a candidate.
articles.body:
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has told the BBC she leads "a brand new party full of new people" - after it emerged in the Spectator , external that the former cabinet minister and Tory party chairman Sir Grant Shapps has been rejected as a Conservative Party parliamentary candidate.

Sir Grant, who has declined to comment, served in nine ministerial roles in government as well as co-chairing the party.

In cabinet, he served as home secretary, defence secretary, transport secretary, business secretary, energy secretary and net zero secretary.

He was also a Foreign Office Minister, housing minister and international development minister , external .

He lost his Welwyn Hatfield seat to Labour's Andrew Lewin in 2024 by 3,799 votes after representing it since 2005.

But his application to stand again for the Conservatives at the next general election has been declined.

One party source told the BBC "it reflects badly on Kemi's temperament. North Korean purges don't work in British politics".

Badenoch told a news conference in central London: "We don't treat our former MPs or our candidates like tittle-tattle for Westminster gossip.

"What I will say is that we're going to be announcing candidates shortly, and you will see that this is a very different party from the one that was removed from government in 2024."

Asked repeatedly about her decision, Badenoch said that "commenting on individual applications would be absolutely wrong" but added that "I want people to know that this is a new Conservative party.

"It is not going to be making the mistakes of the past. We lost 250 MPs at the last election.

"We are changing policies, we are changing people, we are changing process. What I have said is we want people who are going to meet the standards which we are setting. Who are going to abide by the policies I have put red lines on. There could be all sorts of reasons for any individual to be allowed or not allowed on the list."

Badenoch has insisted that future Conservative candidates must agree to abandoning net zero carbon policies and to withdrawing from the European Convention on Human Rights.

It is not thought Sir Grant would disagree with either of these stances.

He also happens to be the co-chair of Conservatives Together , external , a group founded "to support and represent Conservative candidates."

He received a knighthood in Rishi Sunak's resignation honours list for "political and public service."

articles.title: Chris Mason: What his first week in power tells us about Andy Burnham
articles.summary: The fledgling Burnham administration has been seeking to find its feet and make a decent first impression at the same time, the BBC's political editor Chris Mason explains.
articles.body:
"We are on borrowed time if we don't get a move on," Angela Rayner, the former deputy prime minister who is back in the cabinet this week as housing secretary, told the BBC's Today programme on Friday.

It has been quite the week at Westminster. Sir Keir Starmer's departure as prime minister on Monday seems rather a while ago.

The fledgling Burnham administration has been seeking to find its feet and make a decent first impression at the same time, as many try to do in the first days in a job.

There has been an early pattern in these early days: an early morning nugget of news dropping from No10.

On Thursday, it was business rates in England ; on Wednesday, it was bus fares in England and on Tuesday, it was a VAT cut on electricity bills .

Today, the prime minister is assembling what Rayner calls "a pride of mayors" among others for a meeting of what is known as the National Economic Council at the new No 10 North in Manchester.

Andy Burnham claims his new base in Manchester represents the beginning of " the biggest rebalancing of power our country has seen , external " and he will be "bringing forward the biggest changes in the last 40 years".

His early announcements have been considerably more piecemeal than that â he says his "10 year plan for Britain" will come later in the year.

It is worth remembering there was talk from both Boris Johnson and his allies and from Sir Keir Starmer about their plans for the decade ahead â both fizzled out rather more quickly than that.

So how should we assess how much politics has changed, or not?

The early evidence - and let's be frank, it is only that given we are just a few days in - points to Andy Burnham being both more sharp and more nimble than his predecessor in setting out what he is attempting to do and trying to point to early examples of what that might look like, with the announcements of the last few days.

With the tinkering of how the government is run, like the creation of the Office of Prime Minister, and the establishment of No 10 North, he's made it clear that the arteries of power flow very much to and from him.

He hopes he can overcome the critique of Sir Keir Starmer and others, that one of the frustrations of being prime minister can be pulling levers and nothing actually happens.

Burnham's opponents are having to recalibrate and work through how they take on a new prime minister.

The Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch's al fresco speech and news conference on a rooftop in central London on Thursday was a tacit acknowledgement that the political terms of trade have changed.

She teased the new prime minister over his informal style â he "seems like a nice guyâ¦I'm glad he's got a sense of humour," she told us, before getting to the essence of her critique, that his offer was superficial, and thin.

"Is that it?" she asked, adding: "He is behaving like he's still the mayor of Manchester. He is now the prime minister of the United Kingdom."

Burnham wants to project a sense that he gets it - the cost of living pressures so many feel so acutely - and he is getting a move on.

But in just these first few days there has been a reminder that life comes at you fast as prime minister.

Firstly, on the domestic front â his intervention on the early release of prisoners in England and Wales, demanding what he calls a "pause", is a case study in the dilemmas of governing: crowded prisons and, so, difficult choices between least worst options â which criminals to free first.

Secondly, on the international front â after Burnham renewed America's permission to use British airbases for what are called "defensive" strikes on Iran, Tehran is claiming those bases are now legitimate targets. And, with the conflict in the Middle East escalating, the oil price is spiking again .

Then there are the huge questions that tumble from Burnham's big promises.

He has pledged, for instance, "the biggest council house building programme since the post war period." How would this be paid for? And what does the promise actually mean?

It is worth a listen to Matt Chorley's interview with Angela Rayner on BBC Radio 5 Live on precisely this point - the housing secretary isn't able to define when the "post war period" ended and therefore there is no numerical target attached to what appears to be a rather bold promise.

And this on the same day that Rayner acknowledging keeping Labour's promise to build 1.5 million new homes in England by 2029 looks rather shaky: she told the BBC it was "a difficult target".

What about defence spending? The new chancellor, John Healey, packed it in as defence secretary because he thought the department he now runs, the Treasury, didn't get it when it came to keeping us safe.

Let's see how he gets on now the boot is on the other foot.

Burnham is cutting business rates for some in England, but what of Labour's promise in its manifesto two years ago to "replace the business rates system, so we can raise the same revenue but in a fairer way." Will that happen?

And beyond the symbolism of having a prime ministerial office outside London, what, in practical terms, can No10 North actually achieve? How much clout and authority is it given? Just how often will senior ministers be there? And how much will it cost?

Civil servants are being asked if they would like to relocate to the north west of England. The indications from Team Burnham is they take it hugely seriously, but does the civil service truly respond to that, and given the turbulence in politics in recent years, is it an idea that lives beyond this prime minister?

Given the intended long term home of No 10 North is currently a building site and is not due to be finished until 2032 , this is a live question.

Burnham has big ideas - but what will they cost? Published 20 July

Burnham has big ideas - but what will they cost?

And how many noises off do we hear from grumpy Starmerites as the early novelty of governing dilutes? Given the speed with which one, Darren Jones, went public with a grumble it will be something Team Burnham will be wary of.

Then, there is the new prime minister's boldest claim of all â that he will be "bringing forward the biggest changes in the last 40 years". Really? He describes a desire for a "new political model and a new economic model".

It is an understatement to say this triggers a cascade of questions. Including, for some of his critics, including Reform UK, a key one â where is your mandate for doing this?

The fascinating question of the coming months is the extent to which Andy Burnham can credibly or not, as voters see it, set a pathway towards the change he wants and then, in time, call a general election asking for an endorsement of his ideas and direction.

It is three years until there has to be an election, but the timing up until then is in his gift.

His opponents are publicly saying bring it on when there is talk of an election sooner rather than later. Privately, plenty of Conservative and Reform folk acknowledge they are not ready yet.

Could Andy Burnham be tempted? When asked, he has said "we're in a parliamentary democracy and, as we've seen through time, if somebody can command a majority of the MPs in the House of Commons, they obviously then have the legitimacy to lead things forward." That is a statement of constitutional truth, rather than a definitive answer either way to the question itself.

Many prime ministers arriving in office between general elections crave their own mandate. Gordon Brown reflects in his memoirs the agonising private conversations he had about a snap election and in deciding against it found himself going "from near hero to near zero in a day."

Boris Johnson went for it in 2019 and got a near-landslide out of it.

Theresa May, on the other hand, went for it in 2017 and ended up losing the majority she had inherited. The recent history books, then, offer a less than clear guide and Burnham has inherited a colossal majority.

His decision and its timing will likely be driven by how quickly and how much he can do with it.

In other words, whether he is popular enough.

articles.title: Fox News Poll: Democratic enthusiasm shapes North Carolina Senate race
articles.summary: Roy Cooper leads Michael Whatley by 9 points in North Carolina's Senate race, but an enthusiasm gap and Trump's favorability could reshape the contest.
articles.body: In North Carolina, more Democrats than Republicans say they are extremely interested in the midterm elections (51% vs. 42%), and more Democrats also say they are extremely motivated to vote (58% vs. 50%). This enthusiasm advantage creates an edge in the Senate matchup. Democrat Roy Cooper leads Republican Michael Whatley by 53% to 44% in the race to fill the state’s open Senate seat, according to a Fox News poll of North Carolina voters. Cooper’s gap widens to 15 points among those saying they’re extremely interested in the election (57% vs. 42%) and 13 points among those extremely motivated to vote (55% vs. 42%). The race is unchanged among those saying they’re "certain" to vote (53% to 44%). FOX NEWS POLL: COOL YOUR SERVERS! VOTERS REJECT DATA CENTERS Whatley is the former chair of the Republican National Committee, while Cooper served as North Carolina’s governor from 2017-2025. The candidates are vying to fill the seat held by retiring Republican Senator Thom Tillis. Cooper receives high support from moderates, voters under age 30, independents, voters with a college degree, and women. He also captures support from about one in five non-MAGA Republicans and conservatives. Whatley performs best among very conservative voters, White evangelical Christians, White voters without a college degree, and rural voters. There’s also an enthusiasm gap when voters are asked why they back their candidate. Some 52% of Whatley’s supporters say they’re voting for him, while 46% say it’s mainly against Cooper. By contrast, 84% of Cooper supporters say they’re voting for him rather than against Whatley (13%). FOX NEWS POLL: SIGNIFICANT SUPPORT FOR BOTH VOTER ID LAWS AND MAIL-IN BALLOTS Most voters are committed to their choice: 81% of Cooper’s backers say they’re certain to vote for him and it’s 77% among Whatley supporters. Overall, one in five voters say they could switch their pick.  President Trump complicates the contest for Whatley. Forty percent of North Carolina voters view the president favorably and 58% unfavorable. That’s net negative by 18 points, while his ratings were underwater by just 6 points two years ago (47-53%). And Whatley’s ties to Trump concern 48% of voters, with worry extending across the spectrum, including more than half of moderates, more than 4 in 10 independents, and about 3 in 10 non-MAGA Republicans. Meanwhile, concern about Cooper’s ties to the Democratic establishment is more partisan. Overall, 42% are concerned, including 7 in 10 Republicans, but just 3 in 10 independents and moderates. "Recent data put the average Republican advantage in North Carolina statewide races at about 3 points," says Republican pollster Daron Shaw, who conducts the survey with Democrat Chris Anderson. "Cooper’s edge rests on almost unanimous Democratic support and commanding numbers among independents. To win, Whatley must stop the bleeding with non-MAGA Republicans and improve his standing with disaffected, less partisan Carolinians." Personal popularity also sets the candidates apart. Cooper’s 54% favorable rating is significantly higher than Whatley’s at 40%. In addition, Cooper is more popular than the Democratic Party by a 12-point margin, while Whatley trails the GOP by 4. Whatley is less well known overall, as 14% of voters say they’re unable to rate him or have never heard of him, including about 1 in 10 Republicans.  Tar Heel voters share equally negative views of the Republican Party (44% favorable vs. 54% unfavorable) and the Democratic Party (42% vs. 56%). Negative partisanship is strong, as more Democrats view the GOP negatively (94%) than view their own party positively (83%). The reverse is also true: more Republicans (92%) hold an unfavorable opinion of the Democratic Party than view the GOP positively (85%).  Among the small subgroup viewing both parties negatively, Cooper draws twice as much support as Whatley (64% to 32%). Inflation is the top issue for North Carolina voters, with 36% saying it will be most important to their vote for Senate. Next, it’s political divisions within the country at 14%, followed closely by healthcare and immigration at 13% each.  CLICK HERE FOR CROSSTABS AND TOPLINE Half describe their financial situation as stable, 12% say they’re getting ahead, and 38% say they’re falling behind, which is 6 points lower than it was two years ago. North Carolina’s recent voting history points in different directions. Cooper won reelection in 2020 by almost 5 percentage points. In fact, Democrats have won 8 of the state’s last 10 gubernatorial elections. The last Republican to win was Pat McCrory, by about 11 points in 2012. At the same time, Republicans have won the state in 11 of the last 12 presidential elections. The last Democrat to carry the state was former President Obama, who won by 0.3% in 2008.  In the 2024 presidential election, Trump won North Carolina by 3 percentage points. Conducted July 23-27, 2026, under the joint direction of Beacon Research (D) and Shaw & Company Research (R), this Fox News Poll includes interviews with a sample of 1,005 North Carolina registered voters randomly selected from a statewide voter file.  Respondents spoke with live interviewers on landlines (115) and cellphones (654) or completed the survey online after receiving a text message (236). Results based on the full sample have a margin of sampling error of ± 3 percentage points. Sampling error for results among subgroups is higher. In addition to sampling error, question wording and order can influence results. Sources used to develop weight targets include the most recent American Community Survey, Fox News Voter Analysis, and voter file data. Weights are generally applied to age, race, education, and area variables to ensure the demographics of respondents are representative of the registered voter population.  Results among subgroups are only shown when the sample size is at least N=100.  Fox News’ Victoria Balara contributed to this report.

articles.title: Greens review social media operation as Polanski row rumbles on
articles.summary: The Green Party is grappling with how to manage its social media following a controversial post by its leader.
articles.body:
The Green Party of England and Wales is reviewing its social media operation which has been central to its surge in popularity over the past year, sources have told the BBC.

They insist it is not connected to the backlash to Zack Polanski this week after he re-posted a photo of a man wearing a t-shirt with an image of a guillotine and the slogan "we're only making plans for Nigel" - seen as being a reference to Nigel Farage.

But that incident has raised questions about whether it is sustainable for the Green Party leader to manage his own social media channels, with one party figure calling it an "avoidable mistake" and that Polanski "should have said sorry" for it.

In an interview with BBC Newsnight, Polanski repeatedly refused to apologise for "an inadvertent mistake" but acknowledged he needed to "be better on social media".

"I just didn't look carefully enough and I accepted it, as soon as I was aware of what happened I unaccepted it and took it down," he said.

Like other high profile figures on social media, Polanski receives a lot of material from other users seeking re-posts. But unlike most political leaders in the UK, he still manages his own accounts, rather than handing control to party staffers.

This may allow him to appear spontaneous and authentic - both valuable commodities on social media - but it comes with risks.

The current row began after Polanski shared a single post on Instagram that contained a carousel of 20 pictures.

The re-post was shared to Polanski's 713,000 followers, because he accepted a request to tag him as a collaborator, which on the platform makes him a "co-author," placing it on his page and into his followers' feeds.

Polanski said he had not noticed the offending image among the others on the post.

According to him, he had accepted collaborator tags for eight other posts from the same event in Bristol alone.

Reform UK leader Farage claimed the t-shirt amounted to incitement to murder and his party reported it to the police.

Neither the Metropolitan Police nor Avon and Somerset Police say the incident meets the threshold for further action .

But the political row has continued with Reform UK MP Robert Jenrick calling Polanski a "nasty piece of work", at a news conference earlier on Thursday.

Inside the Green Party, there has been some criticism of Polanski's behaviour online.

He has attracted positive and negative attention for the rate at which he posts, comments, likes and replies across multiple platforms including X, Bluesky, Facebook and Instagram.

And this is not the first time a quick reaction has attracted controversy; last month he had to apologise to police after posting about their response to the Golders Green attack.

One senior party source said it was clear that due diligence had not been done on Polanski's social media output, and that moving forwards he needs "tight controls" to stay credible, while keeping a similar tone of engagement with his followers.

They pointed out that the speed and number of Polanski's interactions came with a "small upside" but a "colossal downside", and with the latest incident he had "shot himself in the foot at precisely the wrong time".

It comes as recent polling suggests the Green Party has lost ground to Labour, following Andy Burnham's election as Labour leader, and down from a peak earlier this year.

They added their concerns about a wider problem with the party's vetting on social media and of candidates, including around antisemitic posts in recent months.

Several candidates in recent elections have stood down over their social media activity, with two candidates arrested during May's local elections, and another suspended after being elected.

But Green Party peer and former deputy mayor of London Baroness Jones said the criticism of Polanski's Instagram re-post seemed to be "mainly from our opponents, not internal discussions".

She said that her party leader had "made a mistake", adding "we've all done it and got flak."

But she added: "His online presence is what makes him relatable".

Along with relatability, comes popularity: Polanski is the second-most followed UK leader on Instagram after Nigel Farage. The Greens surpassed other parties to become the most popular on the platform this year.

It is also seen as where a good portion of their voters spend time, as they are the most popular party among the under-30s, according to pollsters YouGov.

One party source said there had been discussions among councillors and activists about whether Polanski was "too online".

"Is he just too online? Is he doing it all himself? Where's the professionalisation here, given the level the party's now grown to, and what people expect of us?" they said.

"There's got to be more checks and balances" the source added.

A separate party source confirmed there was a review going on internally into the party's social media operation, but would not be drawn on whether that meant changing who had oversight of Polanski's posts.

"We are looking at our processes and systems in this area," they said.

"Obviously Zack is really active on social media. It is how we have grown our reach and our membership."

Until around a year ago the party's entire social media team consisted of one full-time employee.

That has now gone up to three or four and may increase further following the review.

"We have expanded hugely as a party and we are looking at how we work," the source said.

"As part of that we are looking at what we might do to support and beef up our social media team."

They said the coverage of the Instagram re-post row had been "deeply irritating" but added that the review was not directly linked to that incident.

But it remains to be seen how much longer Polanski can retain control of his accounts before handing over the passwords to party staffers.

articles.title: Fox News Poll: GOP divisions shape Texas Senate race
articles.summary: Ken Paxton trails James Talarico by three points in the Texas Senate race as character concerns and a GOP unity gap reshape the 2026 midterm battle.
articles.body: President Donald Trump won the Lone Star state by nearly 14 percentage points in 2024, but a new Fox News Poll of Texas registered voters suggests this year's Senate race is far less settled. Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton has yet to fully unify the GOP despite the president’s endorsement in the GOP primary against incumbent Sen. John Cornyn. In addition, more voters are concerned Paxton lacks the character to serve than worry Democratic challenger James Talarico is too extreme, and more Democrats than Republicans are extremely motivated to vote (by 7 points) and extremely interested in the midterms (by 6). Those dynamics give Talarico a 3-point edge over Paxton (51% vs. 48%) in the Senate contest (within the survey’s margin of sampling error). Talarico's advantage in the race grows to 6 points among both extremely motivated and extremely interested voters (53% vs. 47% in each group). FOX NEWS POLL: DEMOCRATIC ENTHUSIASM SHAPES NORTH CAROLINA SENATE RACE Most independents (68%) and virtually all Democrats support Talarico (98%), while fewer Republicans are unified behind Paxton (89%). In part, that’s because one quarter of non-MAGA Republicans back Talarico (24%). Paxton is the choice among White evangelical Christians, White men without a college degree, rural voters, regular worship attenders, men and voters ages 65 and older. Some of Talarico’s best groups are Black voters, moderates, voters under age 30, Hispanic voters, women and voters with a college degree. "Although Paxton dominated Cornyn in the GOP primary, that bruising contest left scars," said Republican pollster Daron Shaw, who conducts Fox News polls with Democrat Chris Anderson.  "He has considerable work to do with non-MAGA Republicans and independents, and that undoubtedly requires aggressively tying Talarico to the Democratic Party’s far left." articles.title: Colorado's socialist surge shakes up the Democratic establishment
articles.summary: A veteran Colorado political insider warned the democratic socialists' rise in Denver mirrors the MAGA movement and could become a cancer for Democrats.
articles.body: Democratic socialist candidate Melat Kiros shocked Colorado’s Democratic establishment when she defeated 15-term incumbent Rep. Diana DeGette in the state's June primary. The double-digit win exposed a growing rift over the party's values that has left some Democrats stunned and questioning the future of the party. "If you had told me this woman would have won by 13 points, I would have bet my house against that," Doug Friednash, a veteran political strategist in Colorado, told Fox News Digital. "I never would have thought we would have seen a victory of that magnitude here in Denver." Friednash has tracked Colorado's political shift from red to deep blue over the past three decades, previously serving in the state legislature representing House District 10 in Denver. He later served as Denver city attorney and chief of staff to former Colorado Gov. John Hickenlooper, and he currently works as a partner at Brownstein, a prominent legal and lobbying firm in the region. Kiros' victory was one of dozens of wins for far-left candidates in Democratic primary elections this cycle as socialists continue to ascend across the country. The far left's rise in the party has alarmed seasoned Democrats like Friednash. JEWISH COMMUNITY IN DENVER ON HIGH ALERT OVER RISE OF DEMOCRATIC SOCIALIST MELAT KIROS "It was one thing watching this happen in New York. ... But when it happens in a state like Colorado, which is really the gateway to the West, it tells me that this issue is going to spread and may be a cancer to the Democratic Party if they don't figure out what our values are," Friednash said. He noted that Kiros' victory did not happen in a vacuum, pointing out that DSA-backed candidates have successfully captured seats in the state legislature and city councils over the past few years. While Friednash originally predicted Rep. Diana DeGette would win, he acknowledged Kiros' campaign had a strong ground game and was able to tap into anti-establishment sentiments among progressives in the region. Kiros' team reportedly knocked on more than 100,000 voters' doors and ran a phone bank reaching 500,000 people leading up to election night. SOCIALISM’S RISE INSIDE THE DEMOCRATIC PARTY NOW THREATENS THE AMERICAN DREAM She also campaigned on fighting for universal healthcare, affordable housing, utilities and more. Friednash said Kiros' message resonated with younger voters who are frustrated by the high cost of living and feel let down by the Democratic establishment. "I think the number one issue is affordability, by far," he said. "A lot of younger people that have moved to Denver have come here wanting to buy a house. They can't buy a home, it seems unaffordable and unattainable. And I think she's tapped into a lot of voter anger and hostility over things not being better." He believes Denver has become a microcosm of the national debate taking place within the Democratic Party over its future direction. Comparing the Democratic Socialists of America wave to the rise of the MAGA movement within the Republican Party, Friednash warned that if party leadership refuses to call out the group's extreme policies, it will ultimately hurt Democrats in swing districts across the nation. RAHM EMANUEL WARNS DSA AGENDA DOESN'T PLAY WELL OUTSIDE 'UPPER WEST SIDE OF MANHATTAN' "As I look out at what's happening within the Democratic Party, you know, it's kind of like a ship without a captain," Friednash said. "A lot of the more mainstream Democrats, rather than trying to say, 'Here are the issues we should be fighting about,' are embracing the socialists  because I think they're afraid of them ... much like I think we've seen with the MAGA movement. "While some Democrats may be falling in love with socialism, you know who isn't? The rest of America," he continued. "That dog's not gonna hunt in these more competitive primaries." Prominent centrist Democratic groups such as Third Way share that anxiety. The organization recently told The New York Times it plans to launch a $15 million campaign to combat the DSA movement, which it believes poses a "mortal danger" to Democrats and will hurt the party in potential presidential swing states. Concerns over the party's ideological turn aren't limited to establishment Democrats. Jon Caldara, president of the Denver-based free market think tank Independence Institute, also questions the future of his home state as democratic socialists continue to rise in prominence. "Without a doubt, the Democratic Party in Colorado has changed," Caldara told Fox News Digital, arguing the state has abandoned its historically pro-business stance. Caldara, a libertarian and longtime radio host and columnist, is outspoken about the challenges facing Denver and the broader state, such as affordability, homelessness and an exodus of businesses. He believes these issues will worsen, warning that establishment Democrats have lost control of their own party. "When the state started turning left, this machine was so powerful, it really couldn't stop itself," Caldara said. "And now it's really beginning to eat their own. It's kind of a French Revolution thing that you see that the Democratic Party here in Colorado is now well out over their skis. And there is a growing fight between Democrats and socialists. "The real telltale is that Democrats are afraid to speak the truth because they don't want to get canceled," he added. "It is vicious to go against the socialists." SHOCKING PERCENTAGE OF DEMOCRATS IDENTIFY AS 'DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS' ACCORDING TO NEW POLL: 'TOXIC POLICIES' Caldara believes younger voters are increasingly being drawn to democratic socialist candidates in Denver and across the country because they lack historical context for how these types of policies have fared across the world. "Sadly, the young suffer from a terrible disease: It's called youth. And because they're young, they haven't seen failed socialism around the globe," Caldara said. "They haven't seen what happened in the Soviet Union. They haven't learned the lesson of Sweden, which looked like such a wonderful socialist paradise until it didn't work, and now they're turning into a capitalist system. They haven't seen this. "So, the idea that we can just redistribute rich guys' money sounds great," he continued. "We'll just do rent control. We'll do government funding. We all know how that's going to end up. It's going to end up poorly. And young people are going to be hurt. "I'm sad that they want to run this experiment again," he added. "And it's even sadder that it's happening in this beautiful free state, this western state, this pro-free-enterprise state of Colorado." Longtime Colorado residents like Gene Maine understand full well why socialist policies are appealing. But having fled the Soviet Union as a teenager in 1981, Maine sees unsettling parallels between the society he grew up in and the direction Denver is headed. As a child, Maine said he was often told that America, Western Europe and capitalism were evil. But as he got older, he realized the utopian society he was supposedly living in wasn't all that it was cracked up to be. REPUBLICANS SOUND ALARM OVER FAR-LEFT GROUP'S PUSH TO TRANSFORM AMERICA INTO 'CUBAN DICTATORSHIP' "As I grew older, I started recognizing that, ‘Oh my God, I'm being lied to. We're all being lied to," Maine recalled. "This is not the freest society in the world. It's a jail." After defecting from the USSR with his mother as a teenager, Maine lived in Los Angeles before settling in Erie, Colorado, in the 1990s, where he’s lived since, raising his family and working as an engineer. Over the past three decades, Maine has watched Denver change from a small "cow town" into a large municipality and witnessed a corresponding political shift as the population boomed. BERNIE SANDERS, DSA REVEAL DEMANDS FOR DEM PARTY AFTER SOCIALISTS SWEEP NEW YORK ELECTIONS "All of a sudden, it wasn't, 'Can we have the smallest government possible and leave us alone?' It became, 'Well, we need to give you free stuff.' And that's when I started to worry a little bit," Maine said. Maine isn't surprised that veteran Democrats are facing primary threats from the far left, noting that Kiros’ campaign benefited from a well-organized ground game and sweeping promises on healthcare and affordability that drew in younger voters. "She is winning the primary because we have an organized group convincing people that they can have free stuff. You can have free medical care. You can have free supermarkets. You can have free transportation. And it's very appealing," Maine explained. "I like free stuff, but what they forget to tell you is that nothing is really free. As they say, there's no free lunch." SOCIALIST HOUSE CANDIDATE SAYS HE AGREES WITH REPUBLICANS ON 'ONE ISSUE' He believes historical lessons are being lost as generations grow further removed from the realities of the Soviet Union. "So, there is a gap that's being exploited," he continued. "And it's been exploited from internal and from external, because there's a lot of evil forces in the world that do not want America to succeed." While critics view the rise of the DSA as a dangerous departure from American values, Kiros and other DSA candidates argue their policies are a pragmatic response to liberal voters fed up with how the Democratic Party has responded to their struggles. Kiros recently brushed aside concerns regarding communists inside the DSA faction of the Democratic Party, telling PBS "Firing Line" host Margaret Hoover there is room in the party for various viewpoints. "Yeah. Well, some members of the Democratic Party are proudly proclaiming themselves as capitalists, and it’s a big tent, right?" Kiros said. "But, again, at the end of the day, it’s up to the voters, right? "Until a self-proclaimed communist actually wins an election, then it’s just noise from the Republican Party. There’s no one who’s actually winning with that." CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE Kiros denied being a communist herself, arguing that younger voters are embracing the DSA message because, at its core, it represents "economic populism." Her campaign centered on Medicare for all, universal childcare, investments in public housing, higher federal taxes on the wealthy, publicly owned utilities and more. Like many other socialist campaigns across the country, she is also firmly anti-Israel.  Kiros' campaign was backed by several progressive groups, including the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), Justice Democrats and the Working Families Party. Republican candidate Christy Peterson, a local accountant, is also running in the Nov. 3 general election, which Kiros is widely expected to win given the district's strongly blue lean. In 2024, Kamala Harris won 77% of the vote in the district en route to winning Colorado. articles.title: Andy Burnham faces unpopularity test over prisons dilemma
articles.summary: The early release conundrum has given the new PM his first taste of tricky political decision-making.
articles.body:
In his first few weeks in Downing Street, Andy Burnham could hardly have been clearer that his aim as prime minister is to make people feel better.

His supporters inside the Labour Party characterise him as a leader with the political nous to prioritise policies that will make a difference, and the communication ability to sell those messages to the masses.

His critics, including Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch, have branded him a "people pleaser" who doesn't want to take difficult decisions.

The conundrum over how to manage the early release of prisoners is an acute example of the tricky political decision-making that inevitably comes with power.

Andy Burnham could have chosen to modify the early release scheme, which he inherited from the Starmer government, according to the length of offenders' sentences.

That would have seen some rapists and child sex offenders released, and inevitably lead to emotive stories from victims whose abusers were being set free.

Instead, the fledgling PM focused on the type of crime, ensuring those mentioned above would stay behind bars.

But that caused a political storm of its own, as it emerged that two of the killers of PC Andrew Harper would still be eligible for early release next year.

That quickly became the first big test for an administration that prides itself on its ability to communicate.

And after mounting pressure from the public, media and members of PC Harper's family, there does now appear to have been a shift.

Burnham said this morning he had "not accepted that it is impossible to do more" to prevent dangerous criminals being released early â and said he's asked the justice secretary to fast-track a plan for freeing up prison places.

He insisted that didn't constitute a change, saying he had been "pushing on this issue" since his first day in office.

But his latest view was not the impression created by the government in recent days.

On Monday lunchtime, Downing Street heavily suggested it could do no more.

Over the weekend, the Ministry of Justice said that exempting more prisoners from early release risked "prisons reaching capacity and collapsing".

And last week, Burnham himself wrote in the Telegraph that he'd "pushed to the very limits of what is possible to do". Justice Secretary Alex Norris even apologised to the families of victims, including PC Andrew Harper.

PC Harper's mother Debbie Adlam told BBC Breakfast the handling of the situation had been a "hash".

Downing Street will hope the events of the last week will be remembered as a PM who has forced the system to do what he wanted.

But they'll fear that the lasting impression could instead be of a misstep that's left victims' families in anguish.

Details of the government's plan to free up prison spaces are still sparse.

The government has been clear that it believes an exemption for manslaughter convictions is an all or nothing approach â and could therefore require a large amount of prison capacity.

Ministers are exploring how to speed up deportations of foreign criminals, the use of female prison spaces for male offenders, and indefinite sentences handed out in past decades.

None of those ideas sound easy, and there'll be questions over whether they will create enough space on the prison estate.

Even if success comes on that front, the PM's statement included an acknowledgement that the difficulties surrounding this policy are not over.

"Even with all these changes, there will be concerns from many victims about who will still be released early for other offences," Burnham said.

When those concerns arise in the coming months, a prime minister who wants to make people feel better may find himself under pressure again.

articles.summary: A suspensão das lives do Discord pela ANPD busca proteger menores e pode resultar em multas de R$ 50 milhões ou no bloqueio judicial do aplicativo no Brasil.
articles.body:
A Agência Nacional de Proteção de Dados (ANPD) determinou nesta quarta-feira (12) a suspensão das transmissões ao vivo do Discord no Brasil. A medida, porém, não significa que a plataforma foi suspensa no país : a decisão atinge apenas a ferramenta de lives .

LEIA TAMBÉM: Agência Nacional de Proteção de Dados suspende transmissões ao vivo do Discord no Brasil

A determinação é preventiva e dá três dias úteis para que o Discord cumpra as exigências da agência. A suspensão vale até que a empresa comprove a adoção de medidas efetivas para proteger crianças e adolescentes .

Se as medidas determinadas pela ANPD não forem cumpridas, a agência poderá aplicar sanções administrativas como resultado da investigação.

Discord — Foto: Discord é uma plataforma de mensagens popular entre os jovens e jogadores de videogame — Foto: Ivan Radic/Flickr

De acordo com o Estatuto Digital da Criança e do Adolescente (ECA Digital), estão entre as possíveis punições a advertência e multas de até R$ 50 milhões por infração cometida .

A aplicação dessas sanções ocorre dentro do processo administrativo conduzido pela própria ANPD.

LEIA TAMBÉM: 'Panelas' no Discord escondem 'as mais perversas formas de crime' contra crianças, diz policial infiltrada

O ECA Digital também prevê sanções mais graves, como a suspensão e o bloqueio de aplicativos . Essas medidas, no entanto, não podem ser determinadas diretamente pela ANPD.

Caso entenda que uma suspensão ou bloqueio seja necessário, a agência precisaria pedir Advocacia-Geral da União (AGU) que acione a Justiça. A decisão final sobre essas medidas caberia ao Poder Judiciário.

Por isso, a suspensão das transmissões ao vivo determinada nesta quarta-feira não equivale a um bloqueio do Discord no Brasil .

“O Discord não está sendo bloqueado. O que a medida preventiva suspende é a funcionalidade ‘Go Live’, utilizada para transmissões ao vivo em servidores fechados. O nosso objetivo é reduzir os riscos de danos graves ou de difícil reparação a que estão sendo expostas as crianças e adolescentes”, explicou Fabrício Lopes, superintendente de Fiscalização da ANPD.

Em nota, a plataforma informou que está analisando a determinação da ANPD e contestou a caracterização feita pela agência, dizendo que ela não reflete a plataforma nem os investimentos realizados em segurança. A empresa afirmou ainda que não tolera conteúdos que promovam ou incentivem a violência e que mantém equipes dedicadas a identificar e remover conteúdos que violem suas políticas. (Leia a íntegra abaixo).

A fiscalização ganhou força após a morte de uma adolescente de 13 anos no Mato Grosso do Sul. Segundo as investigações, a jovem teria sido induzida a atos de automutilação e ao suicídio durante transmissões em grupos no Discord.

O caso também levou o Ministério da Justiça a apontar falhas nos mecanismos de verificação de idade e de proteção de crianças e adolescentes da plataforma .

Na última semana, a primeira-dama Janja da Silva defendeu a retirada do Discord do ar no Brasil e afirmou que a medida deveria ocorrer “imediatamente”.

Na segunda-feira (10), o Discord apresentou à AGU uma proposta com medidas para reforçar a proteção de crianças e adolescentes na plataforma.

O documento foi entregue após reuniões entre representantes da empresa, do Ministério da Justiça e Segurança Pública, da AGU e da ANPD.

O governo havia cobrado mecanismos de verificação de idade, prevenção de riscos e proteção de usuários menores de idade.

Agora, a empresa terá de cumprir as determinações da ANPD para tentar encerrar a medida preventiva e evitar novas sanções no processo de fiscalização.

“Recebemos a determinação da ANPD e estamos cuidadosamente analisando seu conteúdo. A caracterização do Discord feita pela ANPD não reflete a plataforma que construímos nem os investimentos que temos feito na segurança dos usuários. O Discord não tolera grupos ou indivíduos que promovem ou incentivam a violência. Investigamos rapidamente e removemos o servidor privado, acessível somente por convite, envolvido no caso pouco depois de sua criação, e seguimos cooperando com as autoridades policiais na investigação. Além disso, nossa investigação encontrou evidências de que a atividade criminosa foi coordenada em outras plataformas antes da criação do servidor no Discord e continuou nessas plataformas após os indivíduos envolvidos terem sido banidos do Discord. Temos o compromisso com a segurança dos nossos usuários e contamos com equipes dedicadas em desarticular a atuação desses grupos, derrubar conteúdos que violem nossas políticas e tomar medidas contra os responsáveis por essas condutas em nossa plataforma. Esperamos continuar nossas conversas com formuladores de políticas públicas no Brasil para promover uma experiência online mais segura para todos os usuários, tanto no Discord quanto em toda a internet.”
